The House in Committee of Supply, Mr. Gordon in the chair.
Agriculture-health of animals, $1,500,000.
Before the minister enters upon his estimates will he be good enough to tell the House whether or not the embargo on Canadian store and breeding cattle entering England has been actually removed?

speakeroldname: Hon. W. R. MOTHERWELL (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext:
We do not expect that the removal will be actually operative until about the first of April, when the United Kingdom authorities expect to have all the preliminaries ready to allow of the importation of stores under the provisions of the act. The question of breeding animals, however, has not yet been disposed of by the British parliament. I might first of all answer one or two

Supply-Health oj Animals
questions that were raised on the last occasion we were in supply. The hon. member for Qu-Appelle (Mr. Millar) then and on a previous occasion referred to a practice which, it was alleged, was in vogue in the vicinity of Calgary-at all events, the allegation appeared in the Farm and Ranch Review of that city -with respect to the purchasing of reactors and the re-sale of them to owners of herds that supplied milk to the cities. I think that was the purport of the complaint.

The article that appeared in the Farm and Ranch Review of Calgary states that some people are making a practice of buying old cows at about $8 a head, the inference being that they are acquired in the belief that they will readily react. Then at the proper time they ask for an inspection, and when the cattle react they receive from the government $40 a head compensation. The article states that this practice prevails to a considerable extent around the stockyards of Winnipeg.
In the case of animals sold at the stockyards the indemnities would come from the condemnation insurance fund and not under an item of this kind.

Since this matter was first mooted my deputy took it up with the Veterinary Director General, and I might read a paragraph from a communication of his on the subject:
On January 8th, I wrote to the Editor of the Farm and Ranch Review. As no answer had been received on February 15th, a second letter was sent to him by registered mail. To this letter no reply has yet been received. I enclose copies of both letters.
I think it proper to point out that the dishonest purposes referred to in the newspaper story cannot be achieved as simply as is made to appear possible. Protection to the financial interests of this department is afforded by the fact that no compensation is paid for unimals which reast to the first test in addition to herds under the municipal tuberculosis Order. Dishonesty of the kind is possible only by roundabout methods.
If the animals are purchased in the manner described and, being sold to owners of municipal herds, they react on the first test, then no compensation is given. And this provision is intended to obviate just such a practice as is alleged. With regard to the other suggested practice of buying cattle and holding them until an opportune time for inspection, when they react, I do not see how the owners of such cattle could benefit by this practice if the cattle are grade animals. There is no compensation for grade cattle unless they are tested in conjunction with pure-bred herds. As I have explained, there is no compensation for grade cattle that react on the first test, and it is not likely that people would 
be able, to buy pure-bred animals at $8 or $10 apiece; there are not many people who would sell pure-bred cattle at that low figure. So, I presume that the cows purchased at $8 apiece are grade animals; and if they are it is impossible for the owners to get compensation. If they are acquired in the way described they cannot earn compensation because municipal herds are not eligible for compensation under the first test.	^
Would the minister like me to read the article in full? It is already in Hansard.

I do not think that is necessary. Now, I would refer to one or two other matters while I am about it. It was very gratifying to me to note the objection taken to any reduction in the agricultural estimates, but I endeavoured to make it plain the other day that we hoped to keep up this important service with this reduced amount for the next year. It will be recalled that I spoke of $75,000 or $80,000 being spent in this current year for operating the restricted area in Manitoba. Possibly it would be of interest to the committee to refer to the first report in regard to that restricted area, comprising three municipalities in the neighbourhood of Carman thirty miles from Winnipeg. The Veterinary Director General writes:
A recent telegram from Dr. Hall, who is in charge of the area testing in Manitoba, has reached this office, and it will be interesting to you to hear the progress that has been made. Up to February 21st there have been 255 herds tested, comprising 3.238 cattle, of these 258 reacted, giving a percentage of 7.9.
That is not a large percentage when you take them just as they come, one herd after another.
The staff engaged in this work numbers 12, exclusive of Dr. Hall, who probably is not actually doing any testing himself but supervising and arranging the work of his staff. The area covered comprises a large part of the municipality of Dufferin, and Dr. Hall says that he expects to finish the testing of all the cattle in Dufferin municipality by the 28th instant, and adds that weather conditions have retarded progress.
Because of shortage of funds, for one reason, it is not intended to go ahead next year with any further experiments in this restricted area enterprise. I have explained already that the intention was to gather by an actual try-out, information of what it would cost to clean up a given area. When we had that information we were going to the provinces to see if we could not induce them to co-operate with the federal authorities in tackling this big national work. I might say incidentally that the provincial authorities of British Columbia engaged on the work of compensating for tuberculous animals slaughtered before the Do-

Supply-Health of Animals
minion authorities ever took it up, but it was found to be such an enormous task that the federal government had to come to their assistance and take it in hand . Now the enterprise is so vast and important that all authorities we can get behind it should be induced to co-operate, but we cannot get them to join us until we are in a position to advise them as to the probable cost. We do not contemplate such expenditure next year, and consequently that much can be taken off last year's estimate and still meet the ordinary demands incident to this work. In addition to that, there will be found on the back -of the Votes and Proceedings a resolution indicating the intention of the government to bring in a bill reducing the compensation for pure-bred animals that may be slaughtered on account of being affected with tuberculosis. If that bill passes,-I make that qualification because it did not get through last session; if it had we would not be so short of money this year on this vote; if it passes-it will mean that 8300,000 next year will go as far as $400,000 would this year, or 75 cents next year will go as far in the actual payment of compensation as $1.00 this year.
In the area referred to in the Carman district of Manitoba does the work embrace grade cattle?

Yes, everything that is bovine in character. Another reason is that I think we will have to get along next year with a smaller staff of inspectors, as the work arising in connection with the removal of the British embargo is likely to draw off thirty or forty of our veterinary staff. I expect to have the embargo staff returned inside a year, but in the meantime, we will have only three-quarters of our veterinary staff available for the accredited herd areas. For that reason we purpose keeping up the second examination of all herds that have been tested this year. It is very important that we should do this if we want to clear up those herds that have already been taken in on the first examination.
Did I understand the minister to say that his department is not taking on any new herds this year under the accredited herd system?

No. Somebody said that, but I denied it very emphatically. If my hon. friend will subtract $285,000 from the total of $1,500,000 he will find how much money we will have to work with. When we make allowance also for the lesser compensation which I am proposing in my resolution,
and, for the fact that we will not undertake any further restricted area work, it will be seen how it is possible for us to make this reduction in the vote and still keep up the work.

In reference to the $1,-
500,000	for administration and enforcement of Animal Contagious Diseases Act and Meat and Canned Foods Act, how much of that money was spent on the accredited herd system last year?

I placed that information on the Table two or three days ago, but it may not have come to my hon. friend's attention. Speaking from memory, it was, roughly, $400,000 for pure-bred and $300,000 for grade.
How much of this money was spent in the restricted area work?
We have not that work completed yet, and therefore do not know how much it will cost eventually.
Then the minister is taking on new herds under the accredited herd system?
Oh, yes, we are taking on every herd that is coming along in these three municipalities. We want to get that work done in the winter time as we can do it cheaper then.
But over Canada, generally?	' 6
No, not over the rest of Canada; but we are conducting second examinations.
But you are not taking on any more herds outside of that restricted area?

Yes, that was the
substance of my answer. We are accepting applications, and they will be taken up in older of priority when we get our new vote.

I am very sorry that the minister has seen fit to take this course, because I believe the testing of pure-bred cattle in fact of all cattle, is one of the most important undertakings in Canada to-day, for it affects not only our herds but the lives of our people as well. I am very sorry that the minister has seen fit to restrict the work in this particular.
I have not.

Had I got this idea the other night I* would certainly have opposed his increase for the experimental farms,-

Supply-Health of Animals

that is, if that increase is at the expense of the necessary funds for the testing of cattle. That is one of the most important works his department is engaged in. As a breeder of pure-bred cattle, I would even be willing to forego compensation altogther if necessary, and I would certainly be willing that the compensation per head should be reduced, if by so doing he could extend the work of testing cattle for tuberculosis. I think the compensation for animals destroyed under this act is a very small factor in the whole proposition-, the more important feature is the health not only of the animals but of the people who use the products manufictured from milk.
I sincerely hope the minister will reconsider his decision to cut down his vote and will not restrict this very important work.

Mr. Chairman, I think we
all agree that the accredited herd system as introduced is perhaps one of the best, if not the only means in fact, that can be employed to encourage the ultimate eradication of tuberculosis. It has been clearly shown that any plan to make a clean sweep of tuberculosis over any extended area, such as a state or province, cannot be carried out, simply on account of the volume of work and expense involved. In Massachusetts, New York, Illinois and one or two other states where this great work was undertaken, it was found to entail so much expenditure and labour that it was finally abandoned. Therefore we have adopted the accredited herd system, hoping thereby to create little centres free from disease and at the same time educate the people up to the time when we will be able to take hold of the eradication of tuberculosis on a much larger and more successful scale.
It is very important that this work should be carried on without restriction. We have got our farmers educated to the point where they are anxious to have their herds cleaned up, as is indicated by the large number of entries in this particular line. We have already made arrangements with the United States for the exchange of our cattle from accredited herds on both sides of the line without the usual inspection at the boundary. We have a large market on the American side, and it would be a great pity if there should be any interference with the very valuable trade with the United States in purebred animals at the present enjoyed by this country. There is another point: can we afford to stop it, or even to ease up? In 1922 we slaughtered 488,000 head of cattle in our inspected abattoirs. In 1910 the percentage of tuberculosis animals among those inspected amounted to 2-96; in 1922 tffe percentage amounted to 5-26, a very marked increase

indeed. A still greater increase is apparent in connection with our hogs. Last year we slaughtered something like 1,700,000 head of hogs in these inspected establishments, and it was clearly shown that the percentage of infected animals had increased from 5-26 in 1910 to 21 86 in 1922. Can we afford to ease up on this work of cleaning up tuberculosis in Canada? An enormous wastage is involved, not only in the compensation paid, which is very small, in the cleaning up of accredited herds, but also in the interference with trade and the severe losses incurred in shipping the animals to the packing houses. When we see this large reduction of $285,000 in the estimates for carrying out the work of the Health of Animals branch, we wonder if the high degree of efficiency maintained in the past can be continued under those conditions.
Canada to-day possesses an enviable reputation so far as the health of animals is concerned. In fact, it was shown before the royal commission sitting in London in 1921 to inquire into the embargo question that Canada was the freest country in the world from contagious diseases among animals-surely a very proud position to hold, a position that has been attained through the excellent work done by the Department of Agriculture, particularly the Health of Animals branch, in years past. This reputation is of the greatest value to us, particularly when we begin to export our animals, either in live or in dressed state, to outside markets. In fact, it is safe to say that the strongest argument we had to present before that commission in 1921 was this statement of Canada's freedom from contagious disease. While other factors undoubtedly had a good deal to do with the removal of the embargo, that in my opinion was the pivot on which the whole thing turned.
I should like respectfully to offer to the minister a suggestion or two in connection with work that perhaps is not receiving as much attention in the department as it might. I understand that the department is expending about $32,000 a year on research work, including that of the pathological division of the Health of Animals branch. The men engaged in this work are experts in their respective lines, and in addition to carrying on actual research work their time is taken up in the manufacture of tuberculin, etc, I understand that they have put up sufficient tuberculin and mallein to more than cover the amount of money expended on that particular division. While the tuberculin test is the best test we know of at present for the diagnosis of tuberculosis where no physical symptoms are shown, still, its efficiency has

Supply-Health of Animals
not reached the point where it can tell us just how badly the animal is affected. That is, it does not pick out the animal that would be likely to recover from the disease from the one that might be what we call an open case or a spreader of the disease. That is the very serious drawback to the use of tuberculin. I feel that there are great possibilities for research in this connection; we would probably find that from fifty to seventy-five per cent of the animals affected with tuberculosis might naturally recover. The question might also be taken up of vaccination and immunization of animals against this disease. Here is a tremendous field for work that ought to produce very excellent results. At present we are testing and actually destroying those affected, but we spend very little money on trying to discover a remedy that would place us in a very much better position and save us millions of dollars.
Fortunately, we have in connection with the pathological laboratory one of the most experienced animal pathologists on the North American continent. I refer to Dr. Watson, Chief Pathologist of the Department of Agriculture, whose ability has been amply demonstrated in the past. A few years ago a disease affecting horses broke out on the prairie, known as dourine. Several hundred animals were affected, and the compensation paid ran into thousands of dollars; in one year I think it reached $43,000. This gentleman first made a careful diagnosis of the disease. He was able to carry put a blood test devised by himself whereby he could diagnose the disease before any physical symptoms were shown, and in five or six years he had completely eradicated the disease from the country -surely a very excellent work. Quite recently he has scored another triumph in the carrying on of experimental work in connection with glanders; he has produced a serum in the laboratory in Hull, that gives great promise as a remedy for this disease. Quite recently a case of glanders broke out on a farm in Manitoba, and both the farmer and the medical man who treated him became infected with the disease. There had been no cure for glanders in the human being, so far as was known; it is a disease that is very prevalent in some countries, particularly in Russia. A serum produced by the Chief Pathologist was sent out to Manitoba and used in both these cases, and the farmer is now back at work and the doctor making rapid progress towards recovery. Certainly that is a very satisfactory result from the efforts of this gentleman.
37i
I feel that the pathological division should receive the strongest possible support. You have a man there whose experience and ability it would be hard to dupliciate and who would be quickly taken hold of by others if his efforts are not fully appreciated and if he does not receive satisfactory assistance in his present capacity. Here is a field that promises very excellent results if a sufficient amount of money and proper encouragement are given to this gentleman. I should be very sorry indeed, Mr. Chairman, to see the vote stand in its present position, with that very large reduction of $285,000. I would respectfully suggest to the hon. misister that if he is unable to change the present vote he at least make a very strong effort to have an amount placed in the supplementary estimates that will give proper aid to this very important branch of the Department of Agriculture.

Let me right at the outset thank the hon. gentleman for his exceedingly constructive suggestions and criticisms. The fact that we brought down last year $75,000 in the supplementary estimates for this department is an indication that I am not unfamiliar with the fact that what you cannot get by one bite you can sometimes get by two. So it is not too late yet. We shall know inside of three or four weeks, before the supplementary estimates come down, whether the embargo provisions are not bringing about the change that might be expected, and if the worst comes to the worst, why, I am glad the Finance Minister has heard my hon. friend's suggestion; he will know what it means when I recommend to him and my colleagues that we should get a little more, in view of the altered circumstances in connection with the embargo. That was the situation that arose last year; representations were made by the Manitoba authorities after the main estimates came down, and we made provision for a further amount in the supplementaries. That is why the suplementaries are there. So that without making any promises, all I can do is to say that if I find it is required to keep up the work to the full, I will certainly make the same endeavour to meet the situation as I did last year. I am sure that will meet the expectations and hopes of every hon. member in this committee.
With respect to the member of the veterinary staff, Mr. Watson, who has been successful in discovering a serum for the curing of glanders when man is affected by it, I may say that I feel particularly interested in that discovery. Further it seems to me too bad that we have such primitive surroundings for our excellent staff to work in, but I suppose
580	COMMONS
SupplyJ-Health of Animals
we walk before we run, and it seems to me the surroundings we have and the accommodation must answer for the present. We have just moved our biological laboratory from the Experimental Farm to Wellington street, where we have more accommodation, but after all it is not a public building and it is not suitable. It is better than where it was, and the accommodation over in Hull, to which my hon. friend refers, is not what it should be either, but in time, as we find the financial situation eases up a bit, possibly we may be able to spend a little more in the construction of these very necessary buildings. In the meantime, I may say I was almost affected with glanders and I can sympathize too in the full. We have had cases where men have had glanders and have been cured by this newly accepted method worked out by one of the veterinary staff. The men responsible for building up the staff have established it in pretty good shape in the last few years. I do not want to take any credit myself but I am convinced that there is only one policy to adopt, and that is full steam ahead to the capacity of our finances. To show the committee the experience of the United States with respect to this matter, I may say they are also doing the same thing, having only one limitation, and that is money, and I feel that this is a case where many hands make light work. There are other considerations. For instance, having the municipal authorities as well as the provinces interested in it financially, I think, would produce better results in the end, besides being easier on all hands. I have before me a communication from Dr. Torrance to Dr. Grisdale which reads as follows:
Dr. Mohler, the chief of the bureau of animal industry, in his last annual report for the fiscal year ending June 30th, 1922, states that co-operative federal state tuberculosis eradication had given highly encouraging results. Fully accredited herds had increased in the United States during the past year from 8,201 to 16,216.
There are now fully accredited herds in each state with the exception of California and New Mexico and in these states there are 129 herds with 1,370 cattle and 724 herds with 5,573 cattle which have passed one test respectively under this plan.
Dr. Mohler also states that they had on fyle at the time of his report 35,239 applications from owners of herds for accreditation, which they had been unable to handle, and that these herds contained more than one-half million cattle.
I am informed by my staff that while there were a lot of herds on application at the first of this year, we have caught up during the past year on the applications for accreditation. We have not caught up entirely, but [DOT] have caught up pretty well compared with the condition a year ago, so that we are not

even marking time. We think the work is in better shape to-day than it was one year ago. That is, when you take into consideration that we have taken up a new feature of work in the restricted area, and we are following up the second examination. I am sure the hon. member for Victoria and Carle-ton (Mr. Caldwell), whose heart must be in this as an old practitioner, knows the value of it possibly as no other member of this House knows it. I knew the value of it as a sufferer before there was any compensation for slaughtered animals, and I think the committee should be prepared to assist in extending this work and laying the foundation for a new policy in getting the necessary information to enable us to go, I hope, successfully, to the provinces, to start on a plan to take care of the work in a comprehensive way. We will have our limitations however. It is quite possible if we get the municipalities into this matter of accredited herds to co-operate with the provinces and ourselves, we will find more applications than can be taken care of, judging from the experiences of the United States.
Can the minister tell us how much it costs for the treatment of glanders in Treesbank, Manitoba, and that district?
We will take a note of that, or if the question is put on the order paper it will be better.
The minister has no record of it?

We have not that information. It is a continuous work. I think we can dig it out of the accounts, but there has to be some limitation in the matter of available documents here. I will be very pleased to answer my hon. friend, if he will put it on the order paper.

The minister says the reason he is cutting down this vote is lack of money, but I think the explanation is hardly fair, in view of the fact that he has increased some of the other items. If he had said he cut this out to switch money to some other purpose, we would be able to prove it by the very estimates themselves, but in view of the fact that the estimates are $14,000 more than last year, and that what I consider the most important item under this head is cut down, I feel it is a mistake to switch off from this work money that should be devoted to it, and add to some other branch of the service. I think this is the most important service under the Department of Agriculture. I sincerely

Supply-Health of Animals
hope, as the minister has suggested, that he may bring down a vote in the Supplementary Estimates and that he will continue this work on at least as large a scale as before.
With regard to the restricted area in Manitoba, it is just possible the atmosphere is so much drier in Manitoba than at Hull, that it would be a good plan to locate the restricted area in eastern Canada. I do not think he should locate it in Hull. It would be better in the Maritime provinces where we have a moist climate, but not similar to Hull, because the moisture comes from the ocean.

In discussing this with the staff and the gentleman from Manitoba, who probably in a practical way was the first to draw my attention to it, my first thought was to get some portion of Canada that had a distinct boundary line, so that we could operate within certain distinct boundaries, and Prince Edward Island was my first thought and Vancouver Island my second. We had no applications from either of those and no agitation for it, and as one of them does not like innovations very much anyway I was rather disposed to take-[DOT]
Which one?

I will leave it to my hon. friend to guess. I thought it was best to take it up with the Manitoba representatives who were ready and anxious to try it out. After all, if you suggest it to somebody else, you would not have them enter the work with the same enthusiasm as the province of Manitoba would, who are already anxious for it, have passed the necessary resolutions and have worked up public sentiment ready to go into it. However, when Canada's ship comes in probably, we will be able to take action elsewhere. I would like to see it tried in either of those places I have named, because then we would have a complete boundary line beyond which no contagion would escape.
Has Manitoba contributed anything towards the cleaning up of this area?
No.

I would like to
know whether the proposition to reduce the maximum compensation paid has had the effect of reducing the number of applications?
No.

Has it had any
effect at all?

On the other hand, it was found that the bulk of the evidence went to show that, while cholera was present to a very restricted extent, a considerable number of animals had been slaughtered that were not diseased at all. That was the situation. Mr. Alderson slaughtered thirty-three head of animals, which under examination proved to be all right and fit for food. In view of that, the evidence seemed to indicate that a considerable number more had been slaughtered that would have proved to be all right if they had been salvaged. I think Mr. Alderson should have been allowed to salvage either the entire bunch or none at all. I was not in charge at the time; I do not know what the regulations were, and I have not gone into them intimately enough to know whether a mistake occurred or not. I think, however, the veterinary inspectors felt they went far enough when they allowed Alderson to salvage thirty-three. But having salvaged thirty-three, Mr. Alderson came to the conclusion that they had not cholera at all and that if the rest had been salvaged, he could have got the value of them on the market. There is, however, no question at all that cholera was present, and, further, Mr. Alderson could not prove that it had been contracted by any other means than by garbage. Therefore, on the cholera-affected animals, he was not entitled to any compensation, and the ruling of the department and the officers of the department is strictly and legally right.
As regards the animals that were slaughtered and salvaged, and that proved to be all right, there is presumptive evidence that if more had been salvaged, they would have proved

I should like to refer to the matter that the minister was

dealing with just a few moments ago. I appreciate very much the careful manner in which he has inquired into the case referred to, that of Alderson, who had some 245 hogs slaughtered under the Contagious Diseases Act. This man has received no compensation and as a result he has been practically ruined. He had a large experience in this particular business and it is to be assumed that he knew quite well what the consequence would be if cholera developed in his herd. The minister observed that the case had been taken into the courts and that the man had failed to establish his position. Mr. Alderson endeavoured to show that there was no disease in his herd; he staked everything on that issue. There was the alternative by which, if he could establish that the disease might have been introduced from some other source rather than from garbage feeding, he would have been entitled to compensation. But he said that he was satisfied in his own mind that there was no disease in his herd and that therefore he would undertake to establish his case on those grounds. The judge in his finding points out that the evidence of Mr. Alderson and three or four of his witnesses was absolutely in contradiction to that of the officers of the department; and he adds that he finds it necessary to accept the statements of those who. are experts in the diseases of animals rather than the testimony of the owner of the animals. And the owner not having tried to establish that the disease had been introduced from some other source than garbage feeding, there was no other recourse for the court than to disallow compensation. A post mortem was held on one small pig out of this herd of 245 animals. A few culls from different litters were put into a pen together and it was on one sickly-looking little pig that the post mortem was held. The man pleaded with the officers of the department to allow him to slaughter as many of the animals as he could and dispose of them for food. He was given permission to kill and dress what he could in one day and disposed of 33 of them in this way, every one of which was passed by the inspector. Now, it is remarkable that although the inspectors, on taking the temperature of six or eight of these hogs, declared the animals to be diseased, and to have a high temperature, yet when they were slaughtered no disease was discovered in them. I am not going to argue that there was no disease in the herd. The evidence of the officers has been accepted by the court, and the assumption is reasonable that some of these sickly runts among the culls that were in this pen would be most susceptible to disease if it was introduced

from any outside source. And the returns show that some animals that had been taken to the place a few weeks previously for breeding purposes had died, though other animals that had been brought about the same time and taken away had not developed disease. The assumption, therefore, is that the disease might possibly have been introduced from this outside source, although Mr. Alderson might not be aware of its presence. So that now where disease breaks out, if there are any animals that are free from it and are fit for food they will be salvaged and not be a total loss to the owner.
The man concerned happens to be a resident of the constituency that I represent. But I want to say right here that I interested myself in the matter not by reason of any political services he had rendered me, for he had been a staunch Liberal all his life, but because I had known him for many years and was convinced that he was upright and honourable. I am satisfied that when he went into court to endeavour -to prove that there was no disease in his herd he firmly believed that there was not; and I do not think that the officers of the department showed him the consideration to which he was entitled. He declared in evidence, which I think was corroborated by other witnesses, that he was assured by the inspector that he would receive two-thirds compensation for the animals slaughtered, that he would have his premises cleaned up, and that he would be enabled to go into business again. In short, he is simply down and out. In view, therefore, of his sincerity and his loss which the minister admits, I think he is entitled to some consideration. And the fact that the minister even went so far as to recommend a compassionate allowance would indicate the justice of his claim. If the law as it stands precludes some compassionate allowance being made for a person injured in this way, I think that some steps should be taken to see that justice is done. We
talk about passing an old age pension law and other measures for the relief of the people, and it does seem very hard indeed that a man who is trying to earn an honest living should, by an incident of this kind, find himself absolutely deprived of his means of livelihood. The time is coming when the same principle will have to be adopted with regard to other services.
Before the hon. minister leaves that subject, how much money is spent on the fox inspection?
It was $8,000 last year, and $10,000 is set apart for this year. I have a two-page memorandum in regard to it, if the hon. member for Victoria wishes to read it.

I do not wish to delay the vote, but I call attention to the fact that it is an unwise expenditure of money, in view of the fact that the hon. minister has not money enough to test our cows. He is cutting down important work and branching out into speculation.

I think we have got to develop our farming. I like the thought of new ventures that will enable farming to become more diversified, even if it is only in the matter of fox breeding. Take such a matter as the growing of hemp, flax, tobacco, or the breeding of foxes, or anything that will appeal to the people and give them a diversion, I think it is sound policy to develop these things. I am not a protectionist and I think this industry has proved that it would be wise to lay the foundation for a line of pure-bred foxes, and their registration certificates are recognized in the short time in which they have been recorded as being valid, and they have a high standard already.
With reference to the question of horse breeding, my hon. friend (Mr. Lovie) wanted to know why groups of men purchasing a horse could not get the same assistance as clubs of men renting a horse. That looks reasonable enough, but it opens up the old question which dates back to the early days of the western provinces, when there was a general campaign from there, what we called syndicating horses. A great many abuses grew up, and I think one of the reasons is that they do not want to encourage the old policy of syndicating, but I think the object is not so much to help the man who has two or three stallions. The purpose of the assistance is to help the individual farmer who has no other way of securing the services of a good animal except through the medium of the group-that is where five, six, eight or ten, whatever number there may be, group together and rent horses under the assistance given by the department. Now, the giving of assistance to the individual who finds it impossible himself to buy an animal, is the primary purpose. That means giving encouragement also to incidentally the man who owns the horse, but the primary object is the individual; the man who owns the stallion benefits in a secondary way.
If we were to encourage the men who owned the horses, I am afraid it would help to restore the old syndicating business that I am sure some of my hon. friends opposite me must have run across in their early experience in Manitoba and elsewhere.
I notice there is an increase of $170,000 in this appropriation, and I would like to know whether any particular expansion of the live stock industry is contemplated under the increased vote?

We shall devote
ourselves to a general propaganda, carrying the message of better live stock to the people and then following it up by rendering such assistance as we can, and carrying out hog grading also. It is estimated that our expenses in connection with the hog grading alone will amount to about $50,000. At the beginning there has been a little exception taken to our policy, as is always the case in connection with any new policy-but sooner or later it will be generally accepted as right and proper. When the breeds have so improved as to comply with the standard-to the extent, at least, of 50 or 60 per cent in the matter of "selects"-then the time may
Supply-Live Stock

come when something will have to be done by way of fees to take care of the cost of the work.

In connection with this item I would like to inquire as to the possibility of finding a market for western raised horses. Doubtless the minister is well aware of the fact that in that country we have a great number of surplus horses, and the department may possibly be able to do something in the direc+ on of finding a market for that surplus. Is the minister contemplating taking any action along this line?

There is in the
various eastern provinces a very good market for good sized horses, say over 1,350 or 1,400, but I think there is sufficient market in the province of Ontario to take care of all that class of horses offering for sale. That was the information obtained by the Live Stock branch about six weeks ago; and we have a man in the West now helping to develop that business, and indicating the' portions of Ontario where a sale for animals of that description might probably be looked for. But unfortunately the largest number of animals offering there on the western market are animals weighing about ten or eleven hundred pounds, animals running on the prairie, range horses. Some of them, I suppose, will run from ten to twelve hundred, and some under. We have been endeavouring for over a year to find a market in Europe for such animals. We can find the market, but we cannot discover anybody who is prepared to pay for them-that is the difficulty. There is plenty of demand in countries that are unable to pay, and that is the way in which the matter stands.

In connection with this vote I would like to make a remark or two in regard to hog grading. There is a good deal of dissatisfaction amongst the farmers in connection with the present system of hog grading. I believe those who are alive to the situation realize that hog grading in the long run is going to be the best policy, but they point out this important fact, that in so far as the department's officers are concerned they only grade the farmers' hogs when they go into a stock yard. Now, their contention is that the hogs should be graded after having been slaughtered at the plants. The present system, I am afraid, will never be satisfactory to the farmers until the hog grading takes place in the plants as well.
We believe that the packers
5 p.m. are in a position, by judicious selection after the hogs have

passed into the plants and been slaughtered, to get a good deal more number one meat sent out of the plant than they pay for on the open market, and I therefore suggest to the minister that he should look into this question to see whether it is not possible for him to extend the hog grading proposition so as to provide for grading in the plants as well.

With reference to the market for horses, referred to by my hon. friend opposite (Mr. Gardiner), I may say that there was a carload brought down to the Maritime provinces this year and the farmers there-although a market was found for the animals-were very much disappointed with the character of the stock. It was intimated, in the advertisements of the sales that these animals would be useful * for the purpose of improving our stock, but the Maritime province farmers found that they were just ordinary work horses and not very desirable. However, I believe there is a market in the Maritime provinces for the right kind of horses, that is typical horses, calculated to improve the stock that we have there at the present time.
Some reference was made to the question of fox breeding, and I think that it is only fair to say that possibly from no line of live stock: has the government received such a large amount of money in taxes as it has received through the breeding of foxes. I can name one company in Prince Edward Island that has paid as much as $1,000 a year in income taxes. A very large amount of money has been invested in that industry, but it was only within the last year or two any assistance was given to it. We had loc&l registration in our province which was not recognized in shipping animals across the line into the United States, and it was with a view of facilitating that export that the breeders there asked for live stock records to be started in Ottawa. A small amount has been expended in that way-some $8,000 or $10,000. It is not, however, a free grant to the ranchers, as they consider that the fees that are charged for registration are extremely high. I think it is only fair that it should be made known that the government has received very large amounts in the way of income taxes from the fox breeding industry. The breeders are still paying heavy taxes and suffering from certain handicaps which we feel the government should endeavour to remove. With a view to providing remedies an experimental station has already been started.

I would like to inquire of the minister how many breeders there are

Supply-Live Stock
who are paying such immense income taxes. If the enterprise is such a money making business I do not understand why the government should be called upon for assistance to the extent of $8,000 or $10,000 a year. I know of no farmer in New Brunswick who has been doing anything more during the last three years, than merely meeting expenses, let alone pay income taxes. I am more convinced than ever that there should not be any extra appropriation for this industry when it is in the hands of a few breeders and when, as I said, it is a matter of speculation. I hope those engaged in it are making money, but when they are able to pay such large sums in income taxes it is pretty good proof that 1 was right in the contention I advanced.
The fox industry is not confined to Prince Edward Island at all; it extends throughout Canada, and my prompter tells me that the largest branch is in New Brunswick.
That does not make the matter any better. That is the reason I know about it.

These fox ranches developing throughout Canada, and the work that is being done can be done only by the government. The question is only one of doing the work as we are doing it without any cost; or if we start a policy of fees, we shall have to pass the fee system around to many other things than the foxy fox.
Answering the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Gardiner), I am pleased to note that he agrees with the principle of hog grading. Theoretically, and in practice too in small countries, the method of grading is undoubtedly after slaughter. But that does not seem to be practicable in a country like Canada, where animals are shipped long distances and where the owners do not appear on the scene at all after shipment. In a little country like Denmark, a farmer will load his animals on a cart or some other conveyance and take it to the abattoir. He will then go down town, if there is one there, and do a little shopping. Then, on his way back he will get his grade and money and return home, and the transaction is completed. It is not practicable to do that in Canada; but that is the ideal method if conditions would permit. We have a man now investigating the whole question and also getting information that, I think, will lead in a short time to the adoption of a policy of grading the bacon itself. Grading the live hog is only one of the processes that should be checked up and controlled by grading the bacon, especially for export, so that we may
then know just what relationship exists between the select hog and the select bacon. We have made a nice start on the matter, but we are looking forward to the introduction of new features which experience shows to be desirable.
How many hog graders have we in Ontario at the present time?

Twenty-two, all
told, nine of whom I understand, are in Ontario.
It would not be possible then for them to grade all the hogs that would go on the market at the present time.

My hon. friend
means, grade them before slaughter?
No, after slaughter.

They are graded at all the chief abattoirs and stockyards, where-ever they are slaughtered. I may say that we have in mind making provision that, just as a farmer can have his wheat properly graded by the load, a farmer can ask that his hogs be graded at the point of shipment, but for want of time we have not yet succeeded in bringing that about. We are starting at the large centres. My experience has been that, the farmers generally where there are local markets, have not asked the local buyer or drover to grade their animals, but I think a system can be worked out whereby a farmer can demand the right to have his animals graded, and his animals will be tagged, so that the report of the grade can be sent back, and he will know whether the drover has given him the proper grade.
Supposing a carload is shipped f.o.b. to the packing house, without going on the market, are such hogs graded?
Yes. But as a rule, a drover in the country gives simply a flat price for the whole bunch, unless there are some old derelicts.
Have the weights fixed by regulations for "Selects" and other classes proved satisfactory? I have heard some complaints in that regard.

That is quite a problem. It depends upon whom my hon. friend refers to as the one that should be satisfied. We do not pretend to make grades to suit the present bunch of hogs. What we wish to fix is a set of grades that will suit the buying market, and then our desire is to encourage the people to raise hogs that will fit the grade and have a weight that will meet the demand abroad. Mr. Archibald is over-
Supply-Live Stock

seas now, as I told the House the other night, in order to secure a number of breeding hogs; but he is also going over to Denmark to find out what they have adopted as the proper weights of live hogs to make select bacon, and we shall be able to get some information from Denmark. She is supplying the same market, and with the information received from there and our experience here, we shall be able to arrive at just what constitutes a proper size for a select bacon hog. At the abattoirs the weight runs from 160 to 210 pounds, and this means, not always but generally, nearly 220 pounds at point of shipment. If we can raise this without hurting the quality of the Wiltshire side, I would be in favour of raising it; but we must find out exactly what the market wants. It appears to want a bacon side from a hog running from 160 to 210 pounds, but we shall supplement our information with what we can secure from Denmark before we make any change.

No matter what weight is chosen for the premium hog, it seems to me desirable that the next grade should not have the same maximum weight; it should be higher. On that point, there is more dissatisfaction than on anything else; that is as regards taking hogs out of one grade and putting them into another where the maximum weight for the two grades is the same. The minister, perhaps, has the recommendation of the Council of Agriculture on the matter, and it is worth while considering on that point.
Mr. .MOTHERWELL:	The weight, of
course, does not determine the class of the hog. You can have a chunky hog that will not make good Wiltshire.
This comes out of my investigation of the Winnipeg stockyards. More dissatisfaction seems to arise from the fact that the maximum for the premium hog is the same as the maximum for the next grade.
That is probably because a number of people do not understand what we are aiming at.

Have we really any kind of bacon except the Wiltshire that they are willing to accept in Great Britain? The greatest dissatisfaction in our part of the country over this hog grading is because the farmers who were asked to raise a bacon hog, did not understand that they had to raise a hog that was so hard to raise and to get at as the Wiltshire-side hog. They understood that they were to raise a bacon hog that could be produced out of the breeds that they already

had on hand, and the consequence is that they are so badly discouraged that they are giving up the idea of trying to raise a bacon hog if they have to have the Wiltshire-side hog altogether. It was not understood-and I understand this is the case quite extensively-that they had to qualify for the Wiltshire-side. They claim that the breeds they have will not produce enough of the Wiltshire-side to pay them to undertake raising Wiltshire-side hogs. In many places* about one per cent is as high as they get; in some places, they might get a little more than that; but they claim that it is not worth while to try, and they do not believe they can change the breed of their hogs so as to reach the mark that is set at the present time. But they did hope that they could raise bacon hogs.

There are three brands of Wiltshire-side, leanest being the highest, lean the second and prime the third. So that there is a reasonable variation. I recollect having read of other recognized brands in the Old Country but I do not remember them. These are the standard brands, however. I can understand the difficulty my hon. friend speaks of. For over a year we have talked about the advantages of grading hogs. The matter was taken up a year ago last November by various organizations, local, provincial and federal, and there was worked out the best system that could be devised with the information available. Of course, there is always room for improvement as we acquire more information. But this is the difficulty: too many people expected to have a grade that would fit their hogs and they went back home disappointed. As I have suggested to the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Millar), the idea is to establish a standard to suit the market. This is the day of the buyers' market and not the seller's. During the war everything went in the shape of a hog, because the world was hungry for hogs and everything else eatable. But now the boot is on the other foot and our people are disappointed because they cannot get into the select grade and obtain the 10 per cent extra. They will simply have to try to breed better bacon hogs to meet the export requirements. About 50 per cent of the quality of a bacon hog is due to heredity and 50 per cent is controlled by the feeder. As a rule, unless you have lots of dairy by-products you cannot produce a hog of the best type. You cannot make a Wiltshire-side by turning a hog loose at a self-feeder; especially if it gets the kind of feed the average hog is given. By a properly balanced ration you can produce

Sup-ply-Live Stock
a good bacon hog, using a reasonable amount of dairy by-products in the feed. We have not paid adequate attention to feeding with a view to the production of good bacon hogs. As I say, feeding represents 50 per cent, and breeding the other 50 per cent, of conditions that produce good bacon hogs, and we must endeavour to educate the breeders up to an appreciation of that fact.
Is there any system of government grading, inspecting and stamping of bacon which is dressed in the abattoirs for export, or is this left entirely to the packing houses?

For many years there has been in vogue a system of grading by the packers themselves, who follow whatever system they think suits the market. That also formerly applied to live hogs. This system was satisfactory to the packer but not to the buyer, and therefore we are introducing a system of government supervision and standardization. We hope to introduce a system of government inspection of Wiltshire sides, and we shall thus be able to control the quality of export bacon, so that it shall go upon the market in the approved and recognized grades. We have not taken that matter up yet, but we are progressing in that direction.

The minister says that 50 per cent of the success in the raising of good bacon hogs is due to heredity and 50 per cent to feeding. The grading of hogs is a new thing in this country. Prices have kept up fairly well considering the deflation that has occurred in other branches of agriculture, and grading has not been practised long enough to determine whether or not it will be the success it is expected to be. The prices of beef animals have always been fixed according to quality; and the packers have been buying hogs and doing the grading themselves. Now, however, the government intends to fix regulations under which this grading must be done. A minimum weight and a maximum weight are established, and if the animal weighs 3 pounds over 220, it does not receive the premium. If it is underweight, on the other hand, I suppose it is not entitled to the premium either. But you do not follow that up. A packer may take in an overweight animal and if it is of good bacon type he will probably be able to dispose of it at a select price, so that your system is really of no effect. At the Winter Show at Guelph last fall the grading of hogs was a surprise to people who were interested in the business. In many instances animals that did not grade very highly on foot graded 38
well when dressed, and vice versa. And they were examined by men who were experts in the business. I am not finding fault, but it shows how difficult it is to grade animals.
The only true test is that which is made after the animal is dressed and is in the hands of the packer. The packers have graded carcasses for many years, and the government is now stepping in to do something which in any other business is done by one of the two parties to the transaction. I' take it that the government is undertaking this duty on the assumption that the farmer is not in a position to take care of himself. The hon. member for Strathcona (Mr. Warner) said the farmers were somewhat surprised that some animals were not grading. It is quite evident, I think, to anyone who has been engaged in the live stock business for any length of time, that the proper type of bacon hog is one that cannot be economically fed. It is what one might call a long-geared animal, and that type is not regarded highly by the live stock breeders of the country. I venture to say that you will find in the corngrowing districts of western Ontario, when this matter is put to the test, that the farmers will not raise the kind of hog which it is claimed will produce select bacon in the Old Country. This is one of the things that should be demonstrated at the experimental farms, to ascertain the cost of producing bacon under these conditions from the different types of hogs. Many of the breeds that the people are now being advised to try out may cause disappointment and our breeders may quit the business. And of course you cannot grade hogs if none are raised.
Another factor which enters very largely into the successful raising of bacon hogs is pure feed stuffs. In fact in this connection it is of more importance than anything else that may engage our attention this session. The minister admits that 50 per cent of hog disease is due to bad feeding. We have for years permitted the adulteration of feed stuffs, and the disastrous results following their use have driven many hog raisers out of business. In my part of the province it is impossible to purchase hog feed without finding on the bottom of the sack "Screenings not exceeding mill run." It may be said that the law specifies the quality of feed stuffs and prohibits adulteration. But what is the use of such legislation if the millers do not supply feed stuffs of this standard, but, on the contrary, offer us substitutes adulterated with poisonous weed seeds on which we are expected to raise bacon hogs. Hogs of the type described by the hon. mem-

Supply-hive Stock

ber for Strathcon'a (Mr. Warner) might have the capacity to overcome the bad effects of these poisonous weed seeds, but the bacon hog's constitution is too delicate to resist, and thousands of such hogs have died before reaching maturity. I have pointed out the serious damage which is being done to our hogs by the marketing of these adulterated feed stuffs, and on several occasions I have introduced a bill to prohibit adulteration, but without success. However, that matter will come up very shortly when I shall have an opportunity of discussing it at greater length.
I understood the minister to state that this increase of about $50,000 is for propaganda to stimulate the raising of cattle and hogs. We cannot pick up an agricultural paper today without coming to the conclusion that there is propaganda on foot to try to convince our farmers to follow a certain line of production. For months past every agricultural paper in my province has been loaded up with propaganda to persuade farmers to put their money into a business that is not co-operative at all, but is absolutely a joint stock company. After a great deal of effort in this direction we are now informed that nothing further is going to be done along cooperative lines during the present year. I recall another line of propaganda to which the minister has also referred, namely, the grading of cheese. I notice that right here in eastern Ontario our cheese producers have met together and protested most emphatically against this proposal, yet in spite of their protests steps are being taken to compel them to submit to it. It is all very well to pass laws and frame regulations under them to compel people to do certain things, but unless they find it is profitable to do these things all our efforts at compulsion will be fruitless. I very much fear that this propaganda is not good business. The farmer is a fairly intelligent man as a rule, notwithstanding what some people may think about him. He knows when he is engaged in some branch of his business on which he is making a little money or losing, and if he is not making a profit in any particular line we may be certain that he will quickly discontinue it.
This department has now men over in' the Old Country to purchase a certain class of animals which the department desires our farmers to handle. If they are of the type which I have seen very recently, I am afraid that in many instances they will appeal only to those breeders who are anxious to make money out of the introduction of such animals by the department,-in fact in many instances

these men are simply promoters. We heard a year ago about efforts being made to develop markets for our live stock, and a couple of prominent men were sent to South America for that purpose We have not heard very much so far this session about what they accomplished. I asked a question as to whether one of these parties had been appointed Commissioner of Agriculture. In reply, the minister stated that this gentleman was only temporarily engaged, and I believe he referred to him as his "special messenger" in connection with this live stock business, and that he hoped he would be able to go to South America, but sickness had prevented him accompanying the other gentleman. I hope that a lot of this propaganda is not designed for political purposes, but I rather suspect it is. At the close of last session when I arrived home I was surprised to find that this supposed Commissioner of Agriculture was up in my riding addressing a gathering of Liberals. The chairman of the meeting, a member of the executive of the Liberal party for Ontario, was down here in Ottawa at the close of the session; I knew that. Well this "special messenger" of the minister, addressed a meeting of Grits in my constituency. At the commencement of this session I placed a question on the order paper respecting his standing in the service, and to my surprise I find he is still in the employ of the government at a salary of $6,000 a year with several more thousands for expenses. But my inquiries with reference to his activities in my constituency and in other ridings were not answered by the minister. This is the kind of propaganda that is being carried on, and I am afraid that about 50 per cent of it will be found to be political. I am sorry to think that, I am indeed, but my conviction is that in the province of Ontario there is more camouflage along that line at the present time than ever before. Even the president of our Agricultural College at Guelph came into my constituency and addressed a political gathering there.

speechtext: I would draw the attention of the hon. member to the fact that what he is discussing comes under Civil Government. If he seeks to criticize the actions of some of the officers who come under this vote, he will of course be quite in order.

Mr. Chairman, I
would not like to violate the rules of the House. This item being in regard to live stock, and we having been told that the party I have referred to was engaged to develop a live stock market in South America, if I can show that while engaged for that

Supply-Insects and Pests
purpose he was devoting his time to political propaganda, I do not feel that I have transgressed the rules. However, I shall have an opportunity to deal with this subject at a later date.
When the estimates for the experimental farms were going through the minister informed the committee that the system was being changed to meet the changed conditions in the country, and that efforts were being made to develop live stock depots at our various experimental farms for the breeding of animals to supply the adjacent districts. I assume that part of this money will be used to stock up the experimental farms with these animals. The minister shakes his head?
No; that comes under the experimental farm vote.

I notice that the farmers of western Canada are in a position to avail themselves of the concession granted * to them in respect to what is known as the shipment of carload lots of feeding cattle, whereas the farmers in Ontario are not. Ontario has been the great market for the feeders from western Canada during this past fall, on account of their being practically excluded from the United States and Old Country markets. You can understand, therefore, the unfairness of the present regulation which does not enable the Ontario farmer to have these animals shipped back under as favourable conditions as those available to the western farmer. Another source of injustice to Ontario is that a very small proportion of the male animals distributed for breeding purposes are placed in that province. We have not found any particular fault in that regard, but I have endeavoured to show that so far as experimental farms, live stock and all these things are concerned, practically no encouragement is being given to agriculture in Ontario. The minister will realize that it is not fair or in the interest of those who are shipping their feeding cattle from western Canada to Ontario to find that when they arrive there, very high rates have to be paid on the shipments of the cattle back to the farms. There is another preference given in respect to the shipment of animals for breeding purposes from the live stock markets, but so far as I know that preference has not applied to Ontario. The chief complaint I have, however, with regard to rates is in connection with the carload lots. I hope the minister will look into this matter, if his attention has not already been directed to it, and see that some concession is granted along that line.
Item agreed to.
May I ask the minister what amount of money has been expended in the scrub campaign throughout Ontario ,and whether there is co-operation with the provincial government in that resepct?
I understand that $5,000 has been spent under that head. The provincial departments in the West, and also those in Ontario, are co-operating. The extent of that co-operation is pretty hard to define.
I would like to ask the minister a question in regard to the protection of pure bred stock.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I have to direct the attention of the hon. member to the fact that that item has been carried, after a great deal of discussion.
Agriculture-administration and enforcement of Destructive Insects and Pests Act, $310,000.
Will the minister explain the increase of $70,000? Perhaps he will tell the committee also what progress has been made in connection with the campaign against the corn borer in Ontario.

Nearly all these increases are due to the development of our ordinary activities. In the case of insect pests, there seems to have been increased difficulty during recent years in many parts of Canada. In the East the corn borer has been active, and we have had the grasshopper in the West. The activities under 'this item may be divided into two heads, one botanical and the other entomological. The botanical end of it deals with the following subjects: potato inspection; plant pathological investigation; cereal rust; potato diseases; white pine blister rust; fruit diseases Laboratories are maintained at the following points:	Ottawa, Charlottetown, Kentville, Fredericton, Quebec, St. Catharines, Brandon, Saskatoon, Lethbridge and Summerland. Take the question of cereal rust; we have been looking for the best man we can get to carry on the investigational work in that connection, but the kind of men we need are not available at the prices we offer-prices which, as hon. members know, are not entirely controlled by the department. I suppose that after a while, when we have failed a sufficient number of times to get a proper man as expert on fungus diseases of this nature, we shall be able to get a reclassification that will enable us to offer a salary that will command the best man for the purpose. In the meantime we are doing what we can in this direction with the limited supply of men we have. In the Entomological

Sup-ply-Insects and Pests
branch, activities are carried on in respect to insect pests affecting field, garden and orchard crops, forest and shade trees, and so on. Methods of controlling these pests are studied at the following branch laboratories and field stations, which are maintained out of this appropriation: Annapolis Royal, N.S., Fredericton and Bathurst, N.B.; Hemmingford, Aylmer, and Lake Edward, Que.; Strathroy, Vineland and Port Stanley, Ont.; Treesbank, Man.; Saskatoon, Sask.; Lethbridge and Banff, Alta.; Vernon, Agassiz and Victoria, B.C. The second branch of activity is the inspection and fumigation of nursery stock. In this connection stations are maintained at Montreal, St. John's, Que., St. John, N.B., Montrose, Ont., Toronto, Niagara Falls, Windsor, Winnipeg, North Portal, Vancouver. Then, there is the matter of brown-tail moth control in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Quebec. There is the European com borer quarantine and control work in Ontario. The invasion of this insect pest gave rise to the possibility of a very serious interruption in the development of many of our fodder crops. However, quarantine methods have been employed; the habits of the insect are better understood, and the corn borer menace is not looked upon as being as serious as it was a year ago. We are taking all precautions for the purpose of circumscribing as far as may be the activities of this insect. Then there is the question of apple sucker quarantine in Nova Scotia, and alfalfa weevil quarantine in Alberta.
We have the gypsy moth scouting in Quebec, and the satin moth scouting in British Columbia ; then there is the introduction and distribution of parasites and other useful insects, and the study and control of insect pests by their natural enemies and the distribution of these native enemies. These may look like very strange activities, but when I was at the Agassiz farm I visited the entomological laboratory there and found the men engaged in gathering the cocoons of the natural enemy of the spruce bud worm of the Maritime provinces and eastern Canada. They were catching these little fellows and sending them down here to propagate their species and attack their natural enemies and their natural source of food. That is what keeps the animal world and the plant world properly balanced. When they get too many of one kind something else bobs up and feeds upon it, and thus preserves the equilibrium. We are trying to destroy harmful insects and pests by subjecting them to the attacks of their natural enemies, and we are attempting in this way to take care of these invasions.
What results are you getting in the extermination of the spruce bud worm?

It takes time. The parasitic insects multiply with amazing rapidity. Nature as a rule takes care of these matters. In reference to the invasion of grasshoppers, I believe nature has done as much to take care of the extraordinary invasion in the West, in the way of providing parasites of the grasshopper as all the other agencies supplied by man. But British Columbia is a long way from the Maritime provinces and nature has to be supplemented by the transfer of parasites from British Columbia to the Maritime provinces. I have had the opportunity of transplanting beaver to Saskatchewan and placing them in some of the forests reserves-taking them from their native haunts and putting them on the forest reserve. You would lose sight of them in the jungle and somebody years afterward would discover a dam across the road and then somebody would find the beaver. This practice will manifest itself, but it will take time. It depends on the condition. Then as to the spruce bud worm,-I have this memorandum.
Investigations in eastern Canada have shown that the Spruce bud worm problem is not a purely entomological one, but that it involves the entire administration and management of timber resources. Only by the adoption of the broadest practices in the administration and management of these forests will it be possible to establish conditions necessary to prevent a repetition of this recent catastrophe. Our investigations have awakened a very great interest in this problem among foresters and lumbermen and have resulted in cooperative studies and experiments by forest entomologists, foresters and forest pathologists, through which we can hope to obtain in the future a bud worm proof forest. The losses to balsam and spruce in eastern Canada have amounted to at least 150,000,000 cords which would have been worth in manufactured value billions of dollars. As an indication of the savings which have already resulted from our study in the province of New Brunswick alone, it has been estimated by the deputy minister of the Crown Lands Department of that province that following our studies the cutting of Balsam fir and the salvaging of bud worm-killed Spruce and Fir have been of benefit to the province in the past two years to the extent of hundreds of thousands of dollars.

Do the millers claim that their bran and shorts are pure when they send them out?

No, the law permits their mixture now. It allows the mixture of shorts and screenings; if you want to buy it in its purity you must procure it in small packages certified. There is a certain demand in the United States and Canada for bran in small packages for human consumption. It is known as sanitary bran or something like that. It is also produced in large quantities for the American market. When you buy shorts, however, the law permits a certain mixture. For instance, if you have a hundred bushels of wheat from which you get two bushels of screenings, those screenings go into the bran and shorts which are the byproduct of the milling of that wheat. This mixture is allowed by law, and a good many feeders of hogs are very strongly objecting to the adulteration. The bill that we have under contemplation provides for a standard of purity for bran and shorts. I cannot give the hon. gentleman the full provisions of the bill in advance, but that is what we are aiming at.

I think the sooner those
evils are rectified by the proposed bill the better, because when we sell our wheat we are docked so much for screenings, and the millers have no business to sell those screenings as they do not pay us a cent for them. There

is no evidence so satisfactory as something you see yourself, and I may say that I saw in southern Ontario some time ago shorts with the milling company's brand on the bag, but so much adulterated that young pigs would die before they would touch such feed. The regulations ought to be made a lot more drastic because the milling companies get these weed seeds for nothing and we pay the freight rate on them to Fort William. The following year the act was so amended that it really became inoperative, and since that time, as is well known to all the live stock raisers throughout the country, it is absolutely impossible to purchase good feed because it is not manufactured.
