be put there deliberately. Now it is a very easy matter to remedy this, and a year ago I brought it to the attention of the minister. I received an assurance that the matter was engaging his attention and that something would be done, but being very busy at the time I did not press the question. I did not hear the minister's statement on this subject to-night, and I would therefore like to ask now if there is any intention to amend the Feeding Stuffs Act during the present session so as to prevent the continuation of the practice complained of.

I can recall the
question my hon. friend put last year with respect to the desirability of having pure milled by-products and I expressed sympathy with my hon. friend's view. But we were rushed last year, we could not do everything. As it was, we thought that we did very well for our first session. This year the advisability of having some change has been impressed more and more upon me because of complaints coming in from different quarters, especially with respect to the shorts and the deleterious effect of adulterated feed especially upon pigs. We had a conference the other day with the millers, the consumers and the middle men-those who purchase mill feed- consisting of some eighteen or twenty people. The conference arrived at certain conclusions and I have made certain recommendations to the Seed branch with respect to the amending of this Feeding Stuffs Act. Now, I cannot, at this stage, unduly anticipate what is in that proposed legislation. But I think when I get the consent of my colleagues to bringing it down, and I have not yet had an opportunity of doing that, I can assure my hon. friend that in the amendments a remedy will be found for at least some of the difficulties he has been complaining of. We believe in the purity and standardization of mill products, like bran and shorts, just the same as the flour itself. There is no reason why the public should not get pure commodities, and if they want to do the mixing let them do it themselves. That is all I can say at the present time.

The minister is a practical man and understands this question. Therefore why the millers should be called in in order to have their views embodied in any legislation that may be passed in connection with this matter is a thing which I fail to understand. Knowing something that has transpired during the last few years I am satisfied that the millers are the ones largely responsible for the trouble that prevails to-

Supply-Seed Control
day and for the defects which exist in the present statute. It should be a very simple matter to prevent adulteration, there is absolutely no justification for it, and to have the act remain in its present shape, permitting them to indulge in the practice complained of, is nothing less than a humbug.
Now, I want to point out that this practice has not been a matter of gradual growth as some people may believe. The turning point was reached in December, 1917, when an order in council was passed permitting adulteration to a greater degree than it had been indulged in at any time previously. I will refer anyone who desires to look the matter up to an order in council that was put through on 3rd December, 1917, and which contains section 17 of the Grain Products Act. That section reads:
The presence of presumably vital weed seeds in any form of feeding stuff shall be held to constitute adulteration under the act, when more than 25 seeds per pound, as enumerated in the Seed Control Act of 1911, are present in the feed.
Now the trouble is that the millers are putting in machinery that will devitalize a great deal of this seed and the result is that what the minister has referred to has taken place in many instances. I pointed out, when introducing a bill of a preventive nature, many cases of loss of animals having occurred through this stuff having been fed to them, particularly young pigs. That being
9 p.m. the case the committee can understand the extent of the losses that have been experienced through not getting any benefit from the feed stuffs. Two years ago the millers appeared before the Committee on Agriculture and they were anxious to have a third grade of mill by-products sanctioned, known now as middlings, and what was formerly known as low grade flour. The Agriculture Committee refused to consider the matter and it was absolutely turned down by them, but it has since been sanctioned by regulation and is the practice to-day. The short, simple bill which I introduced in 1919 provided that no adulteration of bran, shorts and middlings should take place. The measure was referred to the Committee on Agriculture and after the very strongest debate, the millers having been heard, a motion was passed to this effect:
Resolved that in view of the serious results from the adulteration of bran and shorts by adding thereto great quantities of weed seeds, both ground and unground annually resulting in the death of many animals and serious injury to the health of others, besides distributing harmful weed seeds throughout the country to the detriment of those who engage in agriculture, this committee would respectfully recommend that immediate action should be taken to deal with this question by passing and putting into effect at the earliest opportunity Bill No. 7, an Act to amend the Adulteration Act.
This act was passed, and it was afterwards amended so that it is virtually of no effect and is now not in the statutes at all. The encouragement of the live stock industry and of agriculture in general in this country is something that must have more attention than it has so far received. I am satisfied that no one thing has done so much to discourage those who are endeavouring to develop the live stock industry as this curse with which they have to contend. They have paid good money for it. Is it any wonder that, under such conditions, you find that the farmers have ceased to raise the hogs that you are endeavouring to encourage them to raise? I can point to scores of well-equipped pens for raising hogs where they do not pretend to raise any at the present time. This is quite a common thing, at least, throughout the older provinces, and this condition of affairs is chiefly due to this trouble. Yet, when complaints are sent in, what do we find? We find the minister tonight acknowledging that these complaints are frequent and serious. Yet the millers are to be consulted and they are going to suggest to the department something that ought to be done in the matter. I can see very easily that that means, if their idea is to be carried out, no remedy is going to be provided for the situation at present existing. To say nothing of the losses sustained through feeding this stuff, the consequence resulting from the distribution of weed seeds throughout the country is another feature that I am not going to touch upon, but it is a very serious one. The weed menace is costing Canada millions and millions of dollars, and steps will have to be taken in the near future to control this difficulty with which we have to contend. The big mills may be perfectly satisfied. It is very difficult to come to any conclusion as to the enormous profits that they must make on this stuff, for which they do not pay anything, because they deduct from the grower of the grain much more than the quantity of the impurities to be found in it. Their contention, when they appeared before the committee of this House, was that they purchased this in the grain and they are justified in disposing of it in that way. This contention of the millers will be found in evidence taken before the Committee on the Cost of Living when the three big milling companies were present. It is absolutely unjustifiable. If they desire to sell this stuff, why not sell it for what it is, namely as screenings? That is the proper way to put it on the market. If
Supply-Seed Control

it has a food value-and it has if it is properly cleaned and taken care of-let them put it on the market in that way instead of mixing it with bran and shorts and having people feed this stuff which, in many instances, does more harm than good. This is something which the minister should deal with promptly instead of entrusting it to the millers, because if he does entrust it to them, the end that is desired will never be attained.

My hon. friend (Mr. Sutherland) was not present when I dealt with this matter a few moments ago but inasmuch as he has brought up a few new phases of the question, including the personnel of the conference, I wish to say that we are following, with respect to this conference and the amending of this act, just the same practice as we do with the amending of all acts. There is no reason that I can see why the millers should be ostracised in regard to this matter. The Feeding Stuffs Act deals, in deed, with many by-products of the mill. From the standpoint of the producer and of this House, we want to get information that can be secured only from the millers. We do not want to pass legislation with which it is impossible to comply. Take the highly technical and complicated nature of the conveying machinery and all the different machinery for the various separations in the mill. I must admit quite frankly that I am a layman in this respect. I know the difficulties are there; but before legislating, I want to know whether I am making conditions and laws with which it is impossible to comply. That does not mean that the millers are going to have the whole question delegated to them. We are simply using them fairly, as we do all interests that are involved in any business in the country. For instance, last year, we had a conference with regard to the Fruit Act and another with regard to the Potato Act. Every piece of legislation that we bring down is preceded by a conference of all those who are concerned especially with it, and that is the first important step towards the successful administration of an act as well as getting it on the statute book. No particular party, whether it be the wholesaler, retailer, producer or consumer of an article is going to get all his own way. The making of a law constitutes the ironing out and harmonizing of the differences that invariably exist between the various parts of the community with respect to the activities in any particular line. I think my hon. friend, on reflection, will see that that is quite right. I am sure he does not want to leave in the committee or on the country the impression that 
we are falling into the hands of the millers; that we are going to be engulfed by somebody, and that this act will turn out to be in the interest, not of the people who are asking for it, the men who buy shorts, but of producers of feedstuffs. Not at all. We think, in ordinary fairness to ourselves, as this parliament must be responsible for the law, if we are to have a.good workable law, all parties concerned should be around the board for consultation purposes. After that is done, I think I can assure the committee that this is a measure that will be referred to the Committee on Agriculture and Colonization, because it is legislation concerning which we can have a long chat as to its various phases, and after we have put it through that fanning mill, if you like to call it so, it will again come before a committee of this House. Then, if there is any monster or joker in it, we can rely upon my hon. friend to diagnose and identify it and help us to dig it out. I think I can assure my hon. friend that when this bill comes down, he will be pretty well satisfied with it, even though the millers will have had a hand in assisting to arrive at the ironing-out process which is necessary before a conclusion can be reached.
At this conference to which the minister refers, and at which the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) and others were present, were breeders of live stock represented?
Yes, two or three very prominent feeders and breeders in the neighbourhood of Brantford, I forget their names at the moment.

We have spent a good deal of time on this question, and the minister has been dragged back to it three times this evening. It is a matter in which we are all interested, and I find that the minister's views and mine coincide very closely. I think I can assure the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) that when the bill comes down, there will not be very much difference between him and those who sit in this part of the chamber, and I would suggest that we might let the matter rest now until the bill comes before the House.

The elaborate machinery the minister refers to is used in grinding up the screenings and packing it into the millfeed as evenly as possibly. That is the whole question in which the millers are interested. The minister knows very well that the live stock industry of the country cannot afford to use this stuff that is put into the

Supply-Agricultural Instruction
bran and shorts. There is no use dilly-dallying with a matter that has been before the House and the country so long and which is so unsatisfactory. I venture to say that the officials of the department are just as anxious as I am that this matter should be brought within effective control. I believe the minister has a splendid staff at his disposal to enforce the law and compel the millers to do what is right. There is another question the minister might answer. Have all the screenings which have been purchased by the department been disposed of? I know that there were immense quantities on hand some time ago, for which, I believe, $35 a ton was paid. It remained in the department for a long time. Has it been all disposed of, and who were the largest purchasers of the surplus that remained after the war?

The surplus has all been disposed of. My hon. friend almost tempts me to go further into the details of the prospective bill, which I should not reveal at this stage; but I can assure him that in future, after that bill goes through, he will be able to get bran and shorts straight without any admixture of any other substance.

Item agreed to.
Grant to the provinces of Canada for the purpose of assisting and encouraging agricultural instruction, grants to be made on a proportionate basis, $900,000.
Will the minister explain the decrease of $200,000 in this item?

In this year expires the ten-year period that was provided for when the original act was passed. Although the average of the grant during that ten years was approximately a million dollars a year, the instalments began with $900,000 and ended, as my hon. friend will see, with $1,100,000. Now, one cannot in these days forecast the requirements and the expenditures of the next decade, but I might point out the coincidence that, as did the previous ten-year period, the present decade starts with a grant of $900,000.
What was spent last year?
The entire grant has always been spent. It is allotted to the provinces on the basis of population.
Are there going to be any changes in the distributing of this grant?
That is, in regard to the services for which it is allowed.
Yes.

Inasmuch as $900,000 will not pay for quite as many services as $1,100,000, there will necessarily be changes. The provinces will have to supplement the grant or the number of services will have to be reduced. That will be a matter for negotiation between the provinces and the Dominion. Changes, of course, are being constantly made from time to time as new activities spring up, or seem to require encouragement. I presume that the less important services will either be dropped or will have less attention paid them. A great many of these services are new, and I have no doubt that in the course of the past decade some will have indicated a great usefulness while others will have revealed a comparative inutility, so that the less useful will, I take it, be dropped. Some changes will therefore certainly have to be made, subject to negotiation between the two contracting parties as to what services will be continued in view of the reduced amount of the grant.
Mr. HARRIS- Have any of the negotiations between those parties been consummated?
No, no negotiations have taken place.

I am sorry that it should have been thought necessary to reduce the grant at all. I do not believe that any work carried on in Canada is of more value to the whole country than the work by means of the money provided under this item. In the report of a committee that is charged with this work in Manitoba it is stated that no single piece of legislation has had a more far-reaching influence than the Agricultural Instruction Act. I know that the work carried on in Manitoba with the assistance of this grant is invaluable. The work of the boys' and girls' clubs, of the women's institutes, and the work that is done in connection with home economics, are of incalculable benefit not only to the people of the country but to all the people of the towns and villages. What is done by the boys' and girls' clubs is valuable beyond any possibility of estimate, and I regret very much that it has been thought necessary to cut down the grant at all. I would rather see it increased.
Is the salary of the Commissioner of Agriculture included in this item?

No. I sympathise with the views of the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) . I have had the duty of administering this act from both1 ends, provincial and federal and I know something of the activities

Supply-Agricultural Instruction
that have been developed under the stimulating effect of this expenditure. I have heard them criticized both favourably and unfavourably, but I feel on the whole that the expenditures have been wisely made for very profitable purposes. I cannot do better than pay a slight tribute to the hon. gentleman who was responsible for their introduction in the first instance, and nothing would please me better than to have the privilege of continuing them for another decade, but we cannot see that far into the future. All I can point out to my hon. friend is that the vote is the same today at the beginning of this new decade as it was at the beginning of the last decade. We have now twelve months to size up the financial horizon and think over the matter, and it gives the provinces too an opportunity to look around and wonder whether they are going to carry on this work in the event of these federal grants being finally dropped. This is not the only federal grant to the provinces, next year another one in respect to roads will be up for consideration. We cannot anticipate what will be done then, but it is quite possible that when the two grants confront us the country will be wanting to know our attitude towards the whole business of federal grants to the provinces.

I submit, Sir, that the hon. minister, having journeyed across the Dominion from coast to coast, and having shown in the handling of his estimates, to us baby members at least, that he has a grip of his department and knows whereof he speaks, surely must have some policy respecting the distribution of this particular item. Surely he can give the committee some idea as to how the money is going to be distributed among the provinces.
I have already told my hon. friend that the money will be distributed in the same way as formerly, but that it is inevitable that $900,000 will not pay for as many services ks $1,100,000.
That is just what I want to know-who is going short on the $200,000?
They will all go a little short.
Will the minister explain on what basis this grant is distributed to the provinces?

There is first a flat rate distribution of $20,000 to each province. That is to protect the interests of Prince Edward Island, which would have been discriminated against had the distribution been on a straight per capita basis. There is also

$20,000 granted to two veterinary colleges, one at Montreal and the other at Toronto. The balance is distributed on a per capita basis, that is, according to population.
The minister has not answered my question in regard to the salary of the Commissioner of Agriculture. Is that included in this item?
No.
Where does the salary paid the Commissioner of Agriculture come in? I can not find it under the head of Civil Government.
It was in the previous vote that has just been passed.

In view of the fact that a year ago the minister stated that the Commissioner of Agriculture was working on the Agricultural Instruction Act to determine in what proportion the federal grant should be paid to the various provinces, he will understand the anxiety of my hon. friend to the left to know what was done in that respect. We were told that this "special messenger " of the minister would possibly complete his duties at the end of six months. I think the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) asked the minister the question a year ago and received that answer. I am surprised that the minister did not inform the committee when the previous item was going through that it included the salary of his "special messenger," as he termed Mr. Duncan Marshall, whom I presume he sent up to my constituency to address political picnics.
I do not think the minister has been very frank with the committee.

Can the Minister of Agriculture tell us whether he thinks this way of paying salaries is better for the country or for the government?

I am afraid I would not be an authority on this matter. I have tried both ways, but it is some time since I have tried this method. It seems to work all right both ways. I have not been sitting in the audience listening to the other man making the explanation, otherwise I might have been able to tell better.

It may be better for the government, but I must say it is not very good for the private member. It does not give us any conception at all whether the department is overmanned or not. Previously we were able to make a comparison, and we were able to tell what kind of men had been taken into the service or taken out of it, but under this system we are in the dark, and that seems to be the position in which the government wants to place us.
Have the salaries mentioned in this item reached the maximum or will there be further increases from year to year?

There has been some increase. There is an aggregate increase in those first eight positions of $600, due to the regularly provided statutory increases. They are all now up to the top salary range, I understand, and that is where they will stand until there is some adjustment in the way of classification by the Civil Service Commission, or some increase in salary, but so long as they remain in that category that is where the salaries will be. They are all at the top.

Before passing from that item I should like to ask if there is any possibility of a change being made in the system. I observe that the deputy minister receives a salary of $5,500 and he has been on the job many years; evidently has reached the maximum, and it is quite evident that very heavy work devolves upon a deputy
minister. It seems quite significant that some of the recent arrivals, whose salaries have evidently been smuggled through in some of the items which have been passed without any comments at all, should receive a higher salary than the deputy minister. I cannot understand this system. I was wondering when I saw what has happened whether this was the new system that is to be developed by reason of the activity of the government yesterday in having referred to a special committee the work of the Civil Service Commission who have control over such matters as these. Is this one of the reasons why the party referred to does not come under the Civil Service Act as these officials do? I think it is a most remarkable thing that the Deputy Minister of Agriculture-after the many years' services which he has rendered and the heavy duties which devolve upon him-should receive less salary than a man who passes his winters at a seaside resort down in Florida, makes trips across the Atlantic, goes around speaking at political picnics, and has a real good time at the public expense. This man, the minister states, is his special messenger.

I can only guess to whom my hon. friend is referring, but there is no doubt as to whom he has reference when he speaks of the deputy minister. Now, I explained last year, I think it was to the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader) how Dr. Grisdale's salary seems to be less than that of the average deputy minister. Dr. Grisdale receives $5,500 in cash, and occupies a rent free house at the experimental farm,. an arrangement entered into before my time. The salary and emoluments are considered to be equivalent to $6,000. I made that explanation last year and my hon. friend is aware of it. I hope he will recollect it next year, and not make a grievance out of nothing.

I notice in reading the Estimates of last year that the estimates of the Department of Agriculture occupied three full pages of explanations wherein the names of the officials, the positions they held under the classification, and the salaries paid to them were set forth. Now the only information we get on the same subject is a mere half page, everybody being lumped together, thus affording no chance of distinguishing one official from another or making a comparison. It seems to me that the minister could very readily furnish us with the information as it appeared last year, so that we might be able to make a comparison, and see what difference there is in each case.

I want to add my protest to that of other members as to the method referred to. If it were the custom to pass these items without asking any questions concerning them I realize that it would be a very advisable method for the minister to follow. But when he is called upon to give those explanations that are necessary in order to enable us to dispose of these votes intelligently it will occupy a great length of time. The information given last year, set out in the manner in which it was, rendered the Estimates much more intelligible to members. As it is now the minister gives us the names of officials and other explanations which go on Hansard. But we have not got that information before us, as we should have, and it is very hard-in fact impossible-to remember all these details when they are not before us in printed form. I must say that I was very much surprised when I turned up the Estimates and found the items set forth in the form in which they appear to-day.

Surely the government have some intelligent reason why this change is made. For years the House has been accustomed to have proper information as to the Civil Service given to it. During the war that information was withheld for a short time owing to the pressure of business and the like, but it was again vouchsafed just as soon as the classification became -sufficiently complete to permit of its being done. Now, the details have disappeared and the House is not in a position to properly consider these items. We are refused information, in so far as these estimates are concerned that we have always got. Surely the government are not here to-day to say that they do not care about this matter one way or the other. Surely they are not here to make a laugh and say that this change goes back to a time when there was proper government. Surely that is not the position of my hon. friends. Surely there is some real reason why this is done, other than a desire to make the passage of the estimates difficult. I suggest the least thing the government can do is to give us some reason for this change. Some one must be responsible for it.

I do not think that my hon. friend (Mr. Motherwell) is, perhaps, treating the committee with that courtesy to which it is entitled. If members will turn to items 153, 154, 155 and 157, relating to public works, they will find the information there displayed in accordance with the practice in previous years-that detail of information which has always been looked upon as a great advantage, and which has the effect of facilitating the

passing of estimates. Now if you turn to Civil Government and these votes of the various departments-customs, agriculture, marine and fisheries and so on-you will find that they have been changed to the mysterious and obscure method referred to without any real reason, apparently, being given. There is really no information given whatever. Now there has been some general policy adopted. This does not apply merely to the Department of Agriculture, it extends to several of the other departments so far as I have been able to judge. Perhaps the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) whose courtesy is always unbounded and whose knowledge of the departments is usually fairly complete, can give us a little information on this matter. Apparently it is a policy and method adopted generally by the government, and not simply by one department. As far as I can judge, it is very unsatisfactory and we ought to have some explanation for the change. I would suggest, before the Minister of Finance replies, if he will extend that courtesy to me, that he should give to members, before we pass any more votes of this particular class, the lists of officials as they were printed last year and the other information formerly presented. It would not take very long, it would, I think, be very acceptable to members generally, and might greatly facilitate the passing of the estimates.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I may say that the object was to present the estimates in a form which, it was thought, would be more acceptable to the House as showing the various grades of salaries. Of course the Estimates as formerly brought down never gave the names of officers. Some hon. gentlemen opposite appear to think that there is a departure in that respect but the Estimates in theit
10 p.m. former shape did not mention the name of any officer; they did mention the rank or the position, and in some departments there would only be a few of the higher officials, the rest being clerks. I am assured by my colleagues who had this matter more in hand that the explanation is the one I have stated. I know the object was to present the Estimates so that at a glance members could ascertain how many officers were getting high salaries and how many were getting small salaries. Whether the change is going to prove more acceptable to members than the former system remains to be seen. If the judgment of the House is that the old system was the better one I am not absolutely determined to insist upon the present arrangement. I repeat, the object was not to conceal anything but simply to enable members to see at a glance how many were high

Supply-Agriculture-Salaries
salaried and how many were low salaried officials.
Is it not a matter of importance to know what work a man does when you are considering his salary?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You will find that a great many, probably the majority of the officials cannot be designated by their work; they take rank as clerks. The higher officials can be designated, such as the deputy minister, the live stock commissioner, or other commissioner, a few cases like that; but you do not designate the work of the majority of civil servants at all-they are clerks and doing the general work of the department. But, of course, the minister must be prepared to state in every case the duties of the office, the salary paid, and if necessary the name of the official whose salary is being voted.

I take it from what the hon. gentleman says that he agrees it is advisable to know what an official is doing before we pay him. If he will agree with me to the extent that we have had a reasonable classification in the past, that ought to be continued.

I would like also to point out to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) that last year we had, not only a description of the position held, but a comparison of the salary with that of the previous year. I remember, if the minister will recall, last year the House, in checking over this list, discovered a number of purchasing agents, I think, two or three in one department, and the result of that was a correction or a promised correction, at least, of an apparent overlapping in the department. All we have now, we are told, is that there is one at so much and three at another salary, without the slightest information or comparison at all. If this was designed-I say this with all courtesy-deliberately to mislead and deceive the committee, I do not know of a better form to follow than this that is now being presented to the committee. On the other hand, I can scarcely conceive of more complete details than we have had for many previous years. In fact for as far back as I have been in this House, namely, fourteen sessions, I do not remember any other system.
Apparently, this is the way we have it-
That is no answer. That is no explanation.

If my hon. friend will let me get through my sentence, I was going to say, if the committee is desirous of
getting out the dual system, we can let this matter stand until we do that. We may not come to Civil Government again for several days. I only want to reiterate what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) has said, namely, that the last thing in our minds, as was suggested by some hon. gentleman, was a desire to smuggle something through. What have we to cover up?
That is what we would like to know.

We want to give this information in the most concise and intelligent way. It is not easy to get a mass of names and figures in the most presentable manner, and as I have already intimated, I do not know which is the better way. I have tried both of them and they both seemed to work until to-night.
This is not working.

How would it be if we just try it out and make some specific request for some specific information in order to see if we can get it? I have a number of names with the positions opposite, and my deputy tells me, while he has not the name opposite on this page or alongside, he can turn to each name that is represented by each particular salary. This may take a little while, but not very long.
The trouble is that when the minister gives out the information, we do not have it; it goes on Hansard.
That is the way with all these things.

Pardon me for interrupting, but I want to make my point clear. I would be the last one to insinuate that the government had anything to conceal; but I must say that we cannot consider this intelligently at all under the present method. The minister gives us the information as to these positions. It will be a wonderful man in this committee who will remember one out of five of them when that is done. The information will be printed on Hansard, but we do not get that until to-morrow. Then, we would have to go to Hansard for the various positions explained by the minister and endeavour to pick them out with the salaries, and that, would be very difficult even with Hansard before us. Moreover, in the meantime, the vote is passed. I hope the minister will accept the suggestion of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) and have this prepared somewhat the same as last year. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) states that we have never had the names.

Supply-Agriculture-Salaries
I do not think that is necessary at all/ Last year, the positions were very definitely classified. There were senior clerks and junior clerks. We found that there were statistical clerks in each department, and I remember last year our honoured leader suggested that we had a Bureau of Statistics that could very well deal with all the statistics of the government, and that we should not have a statistical branch in every department as that constituted a duplication of work. We have no way of judging these things from the list as prepared, and I would not attempt to follow the minister's explanations and expect to remember very much when he was done. We do not have the information until we get Hansard to-morrow, and then it is not in such a useful form as compared with the previous method.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I agree at once that the oommittee should have the information. Whether it has it in the form of the printed Estimates or in another form, is not material. I have no objection to the committee getting information as to every rank, position and salary. There is a change in the method, and I admit it is open to criticism; but there is no desire to suppress information, and I am quite content that all that hon. gentlemen have asked for shall be given, whether in the form of these estimates or in another form I do not suppose is material.

I wonder if the hon. gentleman, whose experience in this House is very long and very valuable, could tell us the reasons for the change from this bid form which appears to be somewhat ancient. The Acting Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) 'told us that this is going back to an old form that was used. I am quite sure that there was a very good reason for the change. I dare say the change is one my hon. friend put in himself; but I would like to know just how far back we have to go for this, because then I am going to find out without much difficulty the real reasons why this very beneficial change was made. As regards information which my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding) tells us we shall have, I would suggest to my hon. friend that that information, if it is to be at all useful, ought to be in the hands of the members for a couple of days before the estimates come up again, so that they may have an opportunity of comparing the votes and making up their minds as to whether the thing is proper or not. In the long run, this will facilitate the passing of the estimates.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I cannot tell my hon
friend when this practice existed before, if

it did. I can frankly say that it never existed in my day. If it was an old practice, it antedated my day. As to the object, I will again say that I am quite satisfied, in conversation with my colleagues, that the only object in the world was to put these estimates in a form which it was thought would be acceptable to the committee. That may have been a mistake, but that was the only object in the world.

One thing that appears to be certain is that the change was made in the absence of my hon. friend who, I am quite sure, had he been here, would never have consented to it. Moreover, we can never get from this miscellaneous bunch of meaningless figures, any information that will give us an intelligent idea of what the vote is for. The minister (Mr. Motherwell) does not at all times show that degree of patience which he rather boasts of being master of. My hon. friend is a little fond, when we interject a question, in the informality of a committee, of reading us a little lecture or of scolding us a little. I want to tell my hon. friend that if he takes that attitude, it will not get his estimates very far on with very much facility.
Who is giving the lecture now?

Since the minister has been in this House, last session and this,- he has been treated with kindness and courtesy. Personally, I am desirous of continuing this attitude; but when he intimates that this information is in any degree satisfactory, he is insulting the intelligence of this committee. I want again to request the Minister of Finance, who is leading the committee to-night, and whose department is very largely responsible for the final assembly of the estimates, if he would do this side of the committee at least the courtesy of having brought down, before these Civil Government estimates are up again, simply a reprint of last year. The forms, I venture to say, are in the Printing bureau today. I know something about arranging documents of this kind for printing. I know and I invite the attention of the Minister of Finance to this-it costs a great deal more in time and money to rearrange these estimates in this obscure fashion than to have them reprinted in the fashion of last year. I cannot conceive of any reason whatever for presenting them in this form, if there was a desire to give the information in a clear and frank manner. I will repeat, if the Minister of Finance would agree to bring down these details simply in the form in which we had them last year, this would facilitate very much the passing of these estimates.

Standing Committees

I do not mind taking my little curtain lecture from my hon. friend, but I think he tried to pick me up before I fell. I started to make a statement and before I could say anything he- interjected that that was no answer. Well, I was taking my breath about that time and was coming to the point that if it was the wish of the committee we could stop and take the matter up on another occasion; and that is interpreted by my hon. friend as being not quite courteous. I do not pretend to be an authority on the proprieties or on the question of what constitutes courtesy, but I do not see anything the matter with the suggestion that we could stop now and bring down later exactly what my hon. friend wants. As a matter of fact we got along nicely all evening so long as we were on strictly agricultural questions. Now, I understand, this is a matter of bookkeeping. I do not claim to be an expert on that subject, but I do know that when the government adopted this system they thought they were improving on the old method. It is possible that we may not have done so; that is a matter of opinion. It is true, as my hon. friend opposite pointed out. that the members of the committee have not this information before them. But all evening I have been reading information from documents which the members of the committee have not before them but which apparently they had no reluctance in accepting as correct.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend from Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) rather put me in the position of blaming somebody else in this matter. I wish to say that this is a matter in which the Finance department is responsible, and I desire to share the responsibility with my colleagues in regard to the whole subject. The- suggestion as to the form the information will take will receive due consideration.	.
Item stands.

I have the honour
to inform the House that I have issued my warrant to the Chief Electoral Officer to make out a new writ of election for the electoral district of Moose Jaw, which is now vacant in consequence of the judgment of the Supreme Court of Canada, which I tabled yesterday.
